answer: Use show spectrum-monitoring-<name>/<direction>/<center-frequency> [width] [lower-frequency] [upper-frequency] [target-actual-power] [power-actual] [psd-actual]. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode; it is show-only. name is a String (length 0..64); direction is ingress or egress, default egress, and only egress is currently supported; center-frequency is the band slice center frequency in MHz and is managed by the system. width is the received NMC width in MHz, default 50000. lower-frequency and upper-frequency give the Media Channel edges in MHz. target-actual-power is the target power calculated by ATPS, relevant when target-power-setting = auto, default -99dBm. power-actual is the currently received power in dBm, default -99; -99dBm means either the power has not yet been measured (the measurement is done by the OCM on the DGE2 card) or no power was detected / there is no appropriate fiber-connection. In the egress direction the power actual is calibrated at the DWDM Line port output, the same reference point where target power is defined. psd-actual is the calculated Power Spectral Density in nW/GHz with 2 digit precision, default not-applicable, and does not depend on the spectra width. Example: show spectrum-monitoring-1-7-dwdm-line2/egress/191968750

Read the contention-check-status attribute of the super-channel. It reports the Contention Check state, which is set via DNA in openwave mode. Values are pending, success, overridden and failk, with default pending. It is only applicable if openwave-contention-check is enabled at the super-channel-group level; openwave-contention-check takes false or true and defaults to false, so with the default you get no contention result. contention-check-status can be supplied on creation: add super-channel-<name> carriers <value> carrier-mode <value> [label <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [contention-check-status <value>], and read back with show super-channel-<name> [contention-check-status] alongside carriers, carrier-mode, actual-carrier-mode, capacity, spectral-bandwidth and the state attributes. The related line-system-mode attribute indicates the L1 to L0 power control mode and is openwave. Both commands run in Operational or Candidate configuration mode.

-m is the merge flag: Merge configuration, meaning the command will not fail if the entity already exists. The add command for super-channel-group works in merge mode only, so the -m flag performs a best effort add: if the target entity does not exist it is created, and if it already exists it is updated with any attributes present on the add command. The full form is add -m super-channel-group-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <lock|unlock|maintenance>] [auto-in-service-enabled <value>] [valid-signal-time <value>] [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>] [line-system-mode <value>] [openwave-contention-check <value>]. Defaults for those attributes are admin-state unlock, alarm-report-control allowed, auto-in-service-enabled false, valid-signal-time 480 minutes (range 1..7200), line-system-mode openwave. The command runs in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The same -m merge flag is used by comm-channel, whose add is likewise merge-only.

Use show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [status] [supported-subtypes], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. carrier-mode is an acronymized code (handle) indicating the optical carrier line mode 4-tuple, formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>, a string of length 1..15; examples given are 600E.84P, 100X.73U and 325M.66P. capacity is the net capacity of the optical carrier expressed in gbps. client-mode is the digital client mode of the signal mapped into and transported by the carriers within the superchannel, either ethernet or ethernet-otn. baud-rate is the modulated symbol rate (string). application is the optical transport application ID the mode is optimized for, string length 1..15. compatibility-id identifies the compatible carrier modes that can be applied simultaneously. status is the state of the carrier mode. supported-subtypes lists the subtypes each carrier mode supports, string length 0..32, maximum 20 elements.

Use show supported-gain-range-<name>/<gain-range-type> [gain-range-min] [gain-range-max], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode; it is a show-only capability command. gain-range-type selects which range you want and takes low, high or standard. gain-range-min is the minimum settable gain-target for that type of range (standard, low or high) and gain-range-max is the maximum settable gain-target for that same range; both are of type gain-value and have no default, since they are reported by the system per card. The name key is documented as a flag to enable or disable access control with values true or false and default false. So to see the concrete gain limits behind a low, standard or high gain range setting, show the supported-gain-range instance for the entity and read gain-range-min and gain-range-max for that gain-range-type.

Different power profiles are supported to reflect different scenarios when using a card. The user is able to define, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. To see what a card type offers, use show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. card-type is the card type (string) and name is the profile name (string). profile-description is a description of the profile, string length 0..255. power-draw is the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power, expressed as decimal64. default is true or false and tells you whether that profile is the default one for the card type. None of these attributes carry a documented default value; they are read from the card capability data.

The router ID is controlled by router-id-mode on the bgp-instance. router-id-mode is a flag indicating that the router-id is the loopback IP; it takes use-loopback or manual and defaults to use-loopback, so by default the instance takes the loopback IP address. To set it explicitly, choose manual and supply router-id, which specifies the router ID as an IPv6 or IPv4 address; 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6. Syntax: add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], and it can be changed later with set bgp-instance-<instance-id> [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>]. instance-id is a string of length 1..255 and local-as is a number in the range 1..4294967295. Example: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback. Runs in Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode.

On bgp-neighbor the timer defaults are: connect-retry-interval 120 seconds (range 1..65535), the interval between attempts to establish a session with the peer; hold-time 90 seconds (range 3..65535), the time a BGP session is considered active without keepalives or other messages, typically set to 3x the keepalive-interval; and keepalive-interval 30 seconds (range 1..21845), typically 1/3 of the hold-time. negotiated-hold-time is read-only, range 0..65535 seconds, default 0. Yes, you can authenticate the session: secure-session sets the authentication method and takes none or TCP-MD5, default none, and password carries the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII format, a string of 0..80 characters. All of these are settable on add bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address> peer-as <value> ... or later with set. Related read-only state is session-state (Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established, Close, default Idle) and known-errors.

The routes to be advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. If the prefix is not present in the IGP tables, you must configure a blackhole static route for it: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole. That applies to both ipv4-static-route and ipv6-static-route, where special-next-hop takes the value blackhole. Create the advertisement with add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>; instance-id is a string of length 1..255, remote-address is the BGP peer address in IPv4 or IPv6 format (0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6), and network-prefix is a decimal number 1..64 or 128. A maximum of 100 bgp-network managed objects can be configured. Example: add bgp-network-10/2620:38:4001:192::65/3000::2/64

The comm-channel mtu attribute is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, and it is available only when mode is L3. It is an unsigned 16-bit integer with a platform-dependent range: 1280..1500 octets on 1830 GX G30 only, and 1280..9202 octets on 1830 GX G40 only. The default is 1500; for 1830 GX G40 the defaults per interface type are DCN 1518, AUX 1518, AUX2 1518, OFEC-CC 1518, Craft 1518, CHM6 1518 and UCM4 1518. mtu can be given on add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [mtu <value>] or changed with set comm-channel-<name> [mtu <value>]. The related mru is a separate uint16 in range 64..1500 octets, default 1500, also only when mode is L3. mode takes L1, L2 or L3 and defaults to L3. Example: add comm-channel-gcc0 type GCC0 label GCC0 alarm-report-control allowed mtu 1500 parent otu-1-6-1-OTUC4

LLDP is not on by default. lldp-admin-status on comm-eth defaults to disabled, meaning the LLDP agent neither transmits nor receives LLDP frames on the port; the other values are tx-only, rx-only and tx-and-rx. It cannot be modified if mode is L1 (mode takes L1, L2 or L3, default L3). lldp-transmit-interval is the interval to transmit LLDP Tx TLVs, an integer in the range 1..16383 seconds, default 30 seconds. lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects which interface IP address is used as the management address; it must be explicitly set and applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx, with values 1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only) and L0-MGMT. For speed, auto-negotiation defaults to enabled. rate and duplex-mode are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled: rate takes 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum, and duplex-mode defaults to full. Example: set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx

Use set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>], and read it back with show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]; both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, with default disabled. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses as an IPv4 or IPv6 server address; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, and set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3 to do both in one command. This is the global setting. Per-interface enabling is separate: if-dhcp-relay has dhcp-relay-enabled (true or false, default false) which enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface and obeys the global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. It takes manual, dhcp or both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts name servers from DHCP as well as manually configured ones. Configure it with set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and view it with show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. enabled is a true or false flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, default true. search is the DNS-search-suffix name, a String of length 0..64 which must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear it. Individual servers carry their own origin attribute (dhcp or manual) on dns-server. Example: set DNS enabled true

Add a name server with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server. The origin attribute is the DNS address assignment method and tells you where the entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that has been assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address has been manually configured. The default is manual. You can also convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one simply by changing this attribute with set dns-server-<address> [origin <value>]. View it with show dns-server-<address> [origin], and remove an entry with delete dns-server-<address>. All forms run in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp. The global dns object controls whether DHCP-supplied servers are accepted at all, through assignment-method (manual, dhcp or both, default both).

Use the if-dhcp-relay command: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>], and check it with show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. Both are available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. if-name is the interface object identifier, a String of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on this interface and takes true or false, with default false. It obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (it defaults to disabled) and at least one server-address should be configured for the relay to do anything. Examples: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true, and show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled.

By default a new interface is statically addressed and protected. ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive IPv4 and IPv6 packets. protection-mode is the user given protection mode, taking unknown, protected or unprotected, and defaults to protected; the read-only protection-state reports the current state and defaults to unknown. Syntax: add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> [if-description <value>] [protection-mode <value>] [ipv4-enabled <value>] [ipv4-address-assignment-method <value>] [ipv6-enabled <value>] [ipv6-address-assignment-method <value>] [proxy-arp-enabled <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. admin-state defaults to unlock, alarm-report-control to allowed, proxy-arp-enabled to false (DCN interface only). Note that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface.

Yes, that is what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings a destination and its result takes action on configured static-routes. Create it with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action to take when monitoring goes into failed state and takes none or withdraw, with default withdraw, so the route is pulled by default. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, a string with a maximum of 10 elements. destination is the remote host to monitor (IPv4 or IPv6 address) and next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address; the instance will not be active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is 0..60 seconds, default 5. drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1. enabled defaults to true. The static route then shows monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>. if-name is the interface object identifier, a String of length 0..64 characters, and netmask is the subnet expressed as a netmask; only valid netmasks are allowed to be configured. Read it back with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and remove it with delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. The following addresses are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback addresses), and addresses beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental addresses). origin is read-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, defaulting to static. To list the available interfaces, type ? after ipv4-address-. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask 255.255.240.0 and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0

On ipv4-static-route, distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255 with default 1. Create the route with add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. For a discard route, use special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (default blackhole). Blackhole static routes are needed because routes to be advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself; for prefixes not present in the IGP tables you configure blackhole static routes. Other attributes: advertised is true or false, default false, and when set the route is advertised in the routing protocol, for OSPF as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR; origin is manual or dhcp, default manual; interface must be bound to the same VRF as the static-route vrf. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165

It is the same pattern but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. if-name is a String of length 0..64 characters. origin is read-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Type ? after ipv6-address- to see the available interfaces. Runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64

Yes. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>] and set interface to DCN-B. The interface you name must be bound to the same VRF as the vrf given in the static-route key. Example: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B, alongside the DCN form add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN. Defaults on the route: distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual, special-next-hop blackhole. The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. This retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component; there may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor (instance). direction is ingress or egress. address-subtype is the type of management address identifier encoding used in the address attribute. address is the string used to identify the management address component of the remote system, length 0..64, and its purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype takes unknown, if-index or system-port-number. if-id is the interface number as an integer. address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity advertised by the remote system agent, string length 0..128.

They report the same kind of data but from different ends, and they differ in their key. management-address is keyed by lldp-port, direction, address-subtype and address: show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]. management-address-local drops the direction element: show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], and is used to view the management address information from the local LLDP ports (example: show management-address-local). Both run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode and both expose if-subtype (unknown, if-index based on the ifIndex MIB object, or system-port-number based on the system port numbering convention), if-id as an integer, and address-oid as a string of length 0..128. For management-address-local, address-oid is currently an empty string.

Yes, the networking command has a use-as-source attribute: the interface to use as the source address. It is a string of length 0..64 and has no default. Set it with set networking [use-as-source <value>] and read it with show networking [use-as-source]; both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and show networking to view the current networking information. This is the only parameter the networking command exposes.

Use show networking-services. This command shows the list of network services on the node. It takes no command parameters at all, so there is nothing to qualify or filter on the command line; you simply issue show networking-services. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and it is show-only, with no add, set or delete forms.
